extracted.intended_audience: Citizens/voters of New York (ratification debate); general public considering the proposed Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political essays arguing for the proposed U.S. Constitution by explaining the distribution of powers between federal and state governments, the role of the people, separation of powers, and why feared consolidations or abuses are unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal powers are few and defined; state powers numerous and indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government, are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State governments are numerous and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that federal powers are principally external (war, peace, negotiation, foreign commerce) while states retain broad internal authority; used to argue that the federal government will not swallow up state authority because its enumerated functions are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper allocation of federal powers to external objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government will be exercised principally on external objects, as war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce; with which last the power of taxation will, for the most part, be connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the kinds of powers appropriately assigned to the Union and links taxation largely to foreign commerce; implies acceptability of the commerce regulation as a reasonable new federal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments to manage internal affairs of people
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers reserved to the several States will extend to all the objects which, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the lives, liberties, and properties of the people, and the internal order, improvement, and prosperity of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions state governments as guardians of local/domestic concerns, reinforcing why popular attachment will favor state institutions and why consolidation is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different operational prominence in peace vs. war
rubrics_metrics.description: The operations of the federal government will be most extensive and important in times of war and danger; those of the State governments, in times of peace and security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that because peaceful periods will be more common, state governments will generally command more attention and influence among citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution invigorates original federal powers rather than substantially adding new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The change which [the new Constitution] proposes consists much less in the addition of NEW POWERS to the Union, than in the invigoration of its ORIGINAL POWERS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that many powers (war, treaties, finance) already existed under the Confederation; the Constitution merely provides more effective administration rather than expansion of authority, reducing fear of consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce regulation is a limited and acceptable federal addition
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation of commerce, it is true, is a new power; but that seems to be an addition which few oppose, and from which no apprehensions are entertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats the commerce clause as a narrowly perceived new power that does not justify alarm about federal dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate authority resides in the people; governments are trustees/agents
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal and State governments are in fact but different agents and trustees of the people, constituted with different powers, and designed for different purposes... the ultimate authority, wherever the derivative may be found, resides in the people alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the people's sovereignty as a practical check on governmental usurpation; promising that popular sanction will determine which government gains trust and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular attachment favors state governments due to proximity and opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many considerations...place it beyond doubt that the first and most natural attachment of the people will be to the governments of their respective States. Into the administration of these a greater number of individuals will expect to rise. ... By the superintending care of these, all the more domestic and personal interests of the people will be regulated and provided for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that local offices, personal acquaintance, and everyday concerns create a durable popular bias toward state governments, limiting federal ascendancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local bias in representatives limits nationalizing tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The prepossessions, which the members themselves will carry into the federal government, will generally be favorable to the States; whilst it will rarely happen, that the members of the State governments will carry into the public councils a bias in favor of the general government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims members of Congress will still be heavily influenced by state/local interests, so the federal legislature will not readily sacrifice state prerogatives for national aggrandizement.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments have practical means to resist federal encroachments
rubrics_metrics.description: If an act of a particular State, though unfriendly to the national government, be generally popular in that State... it is executed immediately and, of course, by means on the spot and depending on the State alone... The disquietude of the people; their repugnance and, perhaps, refusal to co-operate with the officers of the Union; the frowns of the executive magistracy of the State; the embarrassments created by legislative devices... would oppose, in any State, difficulties not to be despised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details practical instruments — popular resistance, executive/state legislative measures, inter-state concord — that would obstruct federal overreach without requiring extraordinary force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective state resistance would deter federal oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambitious encroachments of the federal government on the authority of the State governments... would be signals of general alarm. Every government would espouse the common cause. A correspondence would be opened. Plans of resistance would be concerted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that a united reaction among many states would present an insuperable political obstacle to federal attempts at consolidation; analogizes to resistance against foreign oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing army scenario unlikely; militia and state institutions are a check
rubrics_metrics.description: The only refuge left for those who prophesy the downfall of the State governments is the visionary supposition that the federal government may previously accumulate a military force for the projects of ambition... To these would be opposed a militia amounting to near half a million of citizens with arms in their hands... it may be affirmed... that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would be speedily overturned in spite of the legions which surround it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses demographic and historical reasoning to argue that a federal standing army could not realistically subdue the militia and state-backed resistance; therefore military overthrow is an implausible route to consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of all powers in same hands equals tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes a normative standard: complete unification of the three departments is forbidden; this is the core of the separation-of-powers concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers does not require absolute isolation between departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the WHOLE power of one department is exercised by the same hands which possess the WHOLE power of another department, the fundamental principles of a free constitution are subverted... [but] these departments need not be wholly unconnected; partial agency or control is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets Montesquieu: partial checks and shared functions (appointments, impeachment, treaty effects) are compatible with liberty so long as no single entity controls the whole of another department's powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical standard: separation as far as 'the nature of a free government will admit'
rubrics_metrics.description: New Hampshire... declares 'that the legislative, executive, and judiciary powers ought to be kept as separate from, and independent of, each other AS THE NATURE OF A FREE GOVERNMENT WILL ADMIT;' ...The principle is qualified by necessity and practical connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses state constitutions as evidence that an absolute doctrinaire separation is impossible and undesirable; the correct standard is pragmatic separation sufficient to prevent consolidation while allowing necessary constitutional connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: State constitutions provide concrete examples of acceptable mixtures of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites numerous state constitutions (Massachusetts, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia) showing various appointments, impeachment trials, ex officio roles, and shared functions among branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides empirical examples illustrating the allowable degree of overlap (e.g., executive appointment of judges, legislative role in impeachment, executive negative on legislation), supporting the argument that the proposed federal structure does not violate the separation principle in a way that threatens liberty.
